docs.title: 1. Constants
docs.text:
Constants are defined inside consts.hat files. They have the following syntax:

const <name>:<type> = <value>

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
math/consts.hat:

const pi32:f32 = 3.14159265
const pi64:f64 = 3.141592653589793

io/consts.hat:

const localhost:str = "localhost"

docs.title: Importing
docs.text:
You can import constants in functions kinds and other constants files.

For single imports:

use(const:math.pi)

For multiple imports:

use(
    const:math.e
    const:math.phi
)

For multiple imports inside a single const:

use(
    const:[
      math.{pi e phi}
      io.localhost
    ]
)

docs.title: 2. Types
docs.text: Types are defined inside custom files located on src/hat_types/ path. There are basically two types of user types: structs and enums. A quantum type can contain classical types as its members/named values, but the opposite is not valid.

docs.title: Structs
docs.text: Definition: a composite data structure, holding a collection of members (or fields) that may have different data types.

docs.title: Syntax
docs.text: type <name> { <member>:<type> ... }

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
Defining struct type:

type point { x:i32 y:i32 }

Using struct type:

// assigning to variable p while declaring it
p:point =.{x=34 y=43}

// assigning to variable already declared
p2:point
p2.{x=15 y=51}

// (re)assigning to individual members
p3<mut>:point
p3.{x=143 y=331}
p3.y=341

// calling it
print(p.x)

Importing:

// single import
use(type:math.geometry.point)

// multiple imports:
use(
    type:math.geometry.point3d
    type:math.trigonometry.rad
)

// multiple imports, single call:
use(
    type:[
      math.{
        geometry.{point point3d} 
        trigonometry.rad
      }
      status.status_t
    ]
)

docs.title: Enums
docs.text: Definition: a tagged union (or enumerated) data structure that can contain a collection of named values, those being simple identifiers or structs, but only one can be in use at any one time. By convention, identifiers are all caps.

docs.title: Syntax
docs.text: type <name> { <enumerator?> <struct?> ... }

docs.title: Examples:
docs.text:
Defining enum type:

type status_t { ON OFF }

type result_t {
    data{
        value:sample_t
    }
    NONE
}

Using enum type:

// declaring and assigning on a variable
status:status_t = status_t.ON
res:result_t = result_t.data.value=...
res2:result_t = result_t.NONE

// assigning on a declared variable
status2:status_t
status2 = status_t.ON

// calling it
print(status_t.OFF)
print(status)

docs.title: Syntax:
docs.text:
fn <name> (<args?>) <type?> { <body?> }

Return has a special syntax sugar: :: prefixed on an expression.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
Defining a type:

fn sum(a:i64 b:i64) i64 { ::add(a b) }

fn print-gt(a:u64 b:u64) {
    if(
      gt(a b): print(a)
      true: print(b)
    )
}

docs.title: 4. Meta-funcions
docs.text: Definition: a function that defines the code behavior assigned to it. There are three kinds of meta-functions: option (or cases), body (or blocks), and option-body (or case-blocks). They have the types associated with them as optn_t, bdn_t and optbdn_t respectively.

docs.title: Syntax:
docs.text: metafn <name> (args) <type?> { <body> }

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
if meta-function (option type):

Defining:

metafn if(options:[opt-body_t]) ir_t { ... }

Calling:

if(gt(a b):a true:b)

pipe meta-function (body type):

Defining:

metafn pipe(args:[expr_t] body:ir_t) ir_t { ... }

Calling:

pipe(var) { double print }  // applies double on var and then print on double's result

match meta-function (option-body type):

Defining:

metafn match(arg:[expr_t] options:[opt-body_t]) ir_t { ... }

Calling:

match(status) {
  status_t.ON:print("on!")
  status_t.OFF:print("off!")
}

docs.title: 5. Modifiers
docs.text: Definition: a function that can change the semantics and properties of its holder.

docs.title: Syntax
docs.text:
modifier <name> (self <arg?>) <type> { <body> }

the <type> must be the same of self.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
& (reference) modifier

modifier &(self) u32 { ... }  // for u32 type
modifier &(self) [u32] { ... }  // for array of u32 type
modifier &(self) status_t { ... }  // for status_t type

// setting a variable `var` of type "reference of status_t"
var:status_t<&>

docs.title: 6. Cast
docs.text: Definition: a type of reflective function and semantics that convert one data into another type. If data is eagerly evaluated (strict), it should convert to target type calling a given function with given cast name and the appropriate argument types signature. If data is lazily evaluated (lazy), it will evoke its evaluation and then the result value to be cast into the target type. It has a syntax sugar * when called, as in: data * type, meaning "cast data into type".

docs.title: Syntax
docs.text: fn cast (data:<type> to:<type>) <to type> { <body> }

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
Casting strict data:

v1:u32 = 42
// now v1 data is cast into u64 and stored in v2
v2:u64 = v1 * u64

Casting lazy data:

@q:@bell_t =.{@s=@false @t=@false}
@sync(@q)
// evaluate lazy data from @q and convert
//   its result as hashmap with key u64 
//   and value bool, storing at res
res:hashmap<%u64 %bool> = @q * hashmap<%u64 %bool>

docs.title: Rule system
docs.text:
Info

Section in progress. More information to be added.

the H-hat rule system governs the specification of the dialects and their well-formedness rules, in which all languages must adhere to be part of the language family. Concretely, the rules are the following:

Classical and quantum entities must be able to coexist in the same program. Quantum paradigm is a first-class entity just as its classical counterpart. It possesses quantum types, literals, constants, variables and functions that are denoted by the @ prefix.

Quantum data must be lazily evaluated and linear, requiring a cast operator to realize it, to consume it and to drop it.

Reflective cast is an operator that takes one data and one type as arguments. If the data is quantum and type is classical, it triggers the realization of the accumulated instructions inside the quantum data, their emission as a Q3L and execution (with measurements) in a target backend, with subsequent sampling outcome being translated into the target classical type according to some rules described in Section 5. The classical type can be a wildcard value when all that quantum data’s fields have been previously cast.

No quantum physics properties such as qubits, quantum states, gates, circuits, pulses, Hamiltonians or measurement are exposed to the user as language constructs. They are handled internally by the compiler, keeping the dialects platform-independent.

Quantum functions must be declarative in nature to keep the quantum model abstracted away from platform-specific definitions. Quantum low-level languages and target backends will define how each primitive quantum function is interpreted. Quantum functions may have classical arguments, and must be accumulated when applied to quantum data. The rule system must fix each primitive’s signature and intended effect on the data model. A reference semantics is future work, with backends implementing against it.

Artefact kinds are the definitional artefacts (types, constants, behavioral definitions) and the companion artefacts (documentation and proofs) which are first-class entities and live in their own specific locations, with specific but dialect-coherent grammars. Compiler passes may trigger them through different model-driven processes.

Companion artefacts are specifically part of the rule system’s model-driven process, being a project’s mandatory artefacts invoked through the toolchain during flagged building and release steps.

docs.title: What is H-hat
docs.text:
H-hat is a rule system, compiler framework, and a statically typed, functional and distributed-system inspired, hybrid quantum-classical programming language family. As an ecosystem, H-hat provides all the infrastructure for dialect builders so dialects comply with the high-level abstraction paradigm and rule system. Users benefit from using a higher-level abstraction language with well-formedness principles and a unified toolchain.

Writing programs with quantum code is as natural as classical code.

Quantum and classical code may coexist in the same program. Quantum paradigm contains quantum types, quantum literals, quantum variables and quantum functions.

docs.title: Why H-hat
docs.text:
H-hat is intended to be used for designing problem-domain programs. Therefore:

  • H-hat abstracts away the physics from the user
  • Focus on the problem domain instead of physical constraints

A new layer of abstraction unveils new possibilities to think and write about problems. That is the core of H-hat ecosystem. Just like Fortran revolutionalized as the first compiled programming language, H-hat hopes that having the capability to think of the problem and not the physics will enable a new wave of development and creativity.

docs.title: How to use H-hat
docs.text: To use H-hat is necessary to use a programming language that implements H-hat. Luckily H-hat ships with Heather, a reference dialect. You can find it at the Heather dialect page.

docs.title: Version 0.3 (2026-2027)
docs.text:
Info

This roadmap page covers what is expected for the version 0.3 release. A more long-term roadmap will be available in the future.

H-hat version 0.3 is expected to bring the first fully working ecosystem, with Heather as a reference language. The following is an overview of the features to be available:

  • Rule system's rules for quantum logic and enforcing constraints
  • Rule system macros to be used in the dialect compiler building
  • Basic compiler logic on data (ownership, borrowing, drop checks)
  • Quantum low-level languages (Q3L) interfaces and quantum backends
  • Heather compiler passes (source to IR, IR to Cranelift, Cranelift's JIT, IR to Q3L, Q3L to quantum backend)
  • Basic typed message passing logic
  • Reflective cast mechanism
  • Minimal compiler diagnostics
  • Minimal CLI and toolchain features for project management

Below you can find features by category. The items are not necessarily presented in order of priority or logic.

docs.title: Rule system
docs.text:
• Rules for quantum data, logic and its behavior (creation, ownership, borrowing, drop, lazy data behavior and realization)
  • Procedural macros and macros for incorporating rules into dialect's host compiler
  • Rules checks on dialect's host compiler
  • Rules internal validation

docs.title: Compiler framework
docs.text:
• Compiler features for including the rule system on dialect's host compiler
  • Compiler features for including data lifetime cycle (creation, ownership, borrowing, dropping)
  • Compiler features for including the typed message passing
  • Typed message passing mechanism
  • Compiler passes for rules checks
  • Compiler checks and diagnostics for users' code
  • Reflective cast mechanism (realization of lazy quantum data)
  • Q3L

docs.title: Toolchain framework
docs.text: • CLI for project management (project creation, files creation, project update, project build, project execution)

docs.title: Heather dialect
docs.text:
• Compiler pass from source code to high-level interemediate representation (HIR)
  • Compiler pass from HIR to mid-level intermediate representation (MIR)
  • Compiler pass from MIR to Cranelift's CLIF and MIR to Q3L
  • Compiler pass from CLIF to machine code and execution
  • Compiler pass from Q3L to quantum backend, execution and output retrieval
  • Typed message passing mechanism
